I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

vignette: Eighteen months ago, during a night rotation at a forward operating base, Mina was assigned to a perimeter checkpoint adjacent to a civilian thoroughfare. The shift began normally, routine logbooks and halogen-lit coordinates, until a man approached under the pretense of verifying identification. The interaction fractured in a single second. Mina recalls the sudden shift in the guard's stance, the scuff of tactical boots on concrete, the torn canvas of her uniform, and the sharp glare of the overhead light bleeding into her vision. Even then, the experience settled in her mind not as a coherent sequence but as a series of isolated frames. When she later tried to reconstruct the hours, the details refused to align into a believable narrative; the sheer intensity of the assault made it difficult to accept that it had actually happened to her, and the images that surfaced felt like they belonged to someone else rather than to her own life. Back at the base, her days as a soldier became a landscape of quiet alarms. In the vehicle bay, the thick scent of diesel and warm fabric pressed against her ribs. During convoy drills, the steady percussion of boots on packed dirt behind her made her freeze mid-stride. At the physical fitness field, the sudden blast of a whistle triggered a sharp intake of breath that she had to consciously regulate. She learned to manage the rising pressure by deliberately steering her attention toward the mechanical checklist of her rifle or the hum of the radio, mentally shifting focus to logistics and supply routes whenever the images began to surface. In the quiet hours, she found herself replaying the checkpoint incident over and over, examining the exact positioning of the guards, the split-second timing of the orders, the precise wording of the exchanges, trying to find a logical fracture that explained how it went wrong. The mental accounting continued alongside her routine, a separate rhythm that ran parallel to the rest of her days. During the same period, she began ordering extra rations in the mess hall, eating more than usual to create a quiet boundary against the noise in her head. Alongside these shifts, other patterns emerged in her daily life. She noticed that she kept circling back to the conviction that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that the guards positioned nearby or the officers in the command vehicle could have intervened, a thought that sat heavy in her chest without resolving. Her marriage, once sustained by shared weekend drives and easy laughter, grew quiet. She stopped answering calls from her relatives, finding the extended family dinners, Sunday masses, and the familiar cadence of Tagalog now too distant; she felt she had lost her connection to her community and culture, as if her place in that web of kinship had quietly dissolved. When she caught her reflection in the armory mirror, the woman staring back moved with a guarded stillness, answered roll calls with a flattened tone, and flinched at sudden movements. She did not recognize herself. The person she has become feels unrecognizable to her. It was the cumulative weight of these parallel shifts that finally brought her to the clinic. She had stopped volunteering for overtime, cited persistent exhaustion during performance evaluations, and noticed her spouse's careful, unspoken distance. The turning point came during a routine field assessment when her body reacted to the whistle before her mind could catch up, and she realized she could no longer rely on her own internal mechanisms to navigate her duties or her marriage. She sits in the intake room now, hands resting on her knees, hoping to untangle the knots without losing herself entirely. She fears that stepping fully into the memory will make it real in a way she cannot carry, yet she is most hopeful that she might find a way to live in her own life again, anchored somewhere between the images she cannot erase and the days she must still walk.
